title: A letter about electricity
hookLine: rabbis answer questions about electricity, organ donation and fertility treatment
carry: responsa reason from the nearest old case

cards: A letter arrives at a rabbi's house with a question no sage in the Talmud ever faced. May an electric light be switched on during Shabbat? Another letter: may a family donate a loved one's organs?

Another: what does Jewish law say about a child conceived with a doctor's help? There's no page in the Talmud for electricity, and no paragraph in the codes for a fertility clinic. The rabbi can't simply look it up.
So the rabbi does what Jewish teachers have done for a long time: reads, thinks, and writes back.

teach.b: Old law. You met this form last year, rulings sent by letter; today, how it meets what's new. First, the form.
The exchange is called she'elot u-teshuvot, questions and answers; in English, responsa. A person or a community writes with a real problem, and a rabbi answers in writing, with reasons.
Collections of these letters line the shelves of Jewish libraries. Second, the method. No verse mentions electricity, so the rabbi looks for the nearest case the old law did discuss.
The Torah forbids kindling fire throughout your dwellings on the Sabbath day.
Is a glowing bulb a kind of fire? Is closing a circuit a kind of building, finishing something so that it works? Or is it something else entirely?
Each answer depends on which old case the new one is most like. Third, the disagreement.

Because the comparison decides so much, careful rabbis reading the same sources can reach different answers. On organ donation, much turns on how the moment of death is understood, and authorities answer differently.
Orthodox rabbis, Conservative law committees and Reform rabbinic bodies all write responsa, each in their own way.
Fourth, the person. A responsum answers someone: a family at a hospital bed, a couple who want a child.

teach.h: REASON FROM THE NEAREST OLD CASE.
teach.b: The law isn't consulted from a distance; it's asked, by name, in the middle of a life. That's why the old law keeps speaking: people keep bringing it questions, and someone keeps writing back.

how: Jews with a question of practice often ask a rabbi they trust. Rabbis answer in person or in writing, and published responsa from Orthodox, Conservative and Reform authorities are collected and studied.

games.q: you're a rabbi. a letter asks whether an electric light may be switched on during Shabbat. no ancient text mentions electricity. what do you do?
o: write back that the law has nothing to say.
find the nearest case the old law discusses, and reason from it.
decide by whatever feels right to you.
games.why: responsa reason by comparison: is a glowing bulb like kindling fire, or like building, or something else? the comparison shapes the answer.

practice: Choose a question your great-grandparents never faced, like whether to answer a work message at the dinner table.
Instead of answering it, ask what older thing it's most like, a letter, a knock at the door, a talk in the town square, and notice how the answer shifts with each comparison.
